As Chairman of ADMA, it is a great honour and privilege to welcome our distinguished guests, Government representatives, exhibitors, and visitors to the ADMA 2026 Agrishow.The Agricultural Dealers and Manufacturers Association of Zimbabwe stands as a strong and properly constituted body, representing a committed membership. At our core, we exist to promote excellence—driving high standards of service and ensuring ethical, transparent trading across the agricultural machinery sector.Our Agrishow is more than an event—it is a platform. A once-a-year opportunity for industry suppliers and farmers to connect, to engage, and to compare innovative products that deliver real efficiency and cost-saving value.Our farmers are the backbone of this country, and their success depends on practical, affordable, and forward-thinking solutions. The adoption of modern farming practices, supported by effective irrigation, is no longer optional - it is essential for sustainability and growth.We have strategically positioned this Agrishow early in the calendar, avoiding overlap with key regional exhibitions such as Nampo in South Africa and Agritech in Zambia. This allows the industry to plan ahead, ensuring that the right equipment and inputs are available for the coming season.Importantly, we remain committed to accessibility. Exhibition space is offered to suppliers of agricultural inputs, machinery, and equipment at highly competitive rates - ensuring that participation is within reach and that value is passed on to our farmers.This year, we have taken further steps toward inclusivity within agriculture. The livestock section has been expanded, with both cattle and sheep now playing a more prominent role. The animals on display are pedigree stock, registered with the Zimbabwe Herd Book, with a strong focus on indigenous breeds - genetics that have been shaped by generations of resilience in Africa’s challenging conditions. These are assets we must preserve and protect.To all our exhibitors - thank you. Your continued support and partnership are what make this platform possible and impactful.I also extend my sincere appreciation to the executive of the Agricultural Research Trust, to my committee, and to all ADMA members for your unwavering support and commitment throughout my term of office.Ladies and gentlemen, agriculture is not just an industry - it is our foundation, our future, and our responsibility. Let us use this Agrishow to innovate, to collaborate, and to drive Zimbabwean agriculture forward - together.
CHAIRMAN

The Agricultural Research Trust (ART) Farm is excited once again to host the return of the ADMA (Agricultural Dealers and Manufacturers Association) Agrishow from June 4 to June 6, 2026.

This event will once again offer the country’s agricultural sector key stakeholder’s international visitors and exhibitors, as well as the public, access to a wide variety of agricultural services, products and equipment, all industry professionals and suppliers all gathered at the ADMA Agrishow ART Farm premises, forming a distinctive and exciting agricultural experience.The ADMA Agrishow extends beyond the agricultural sector alone; we highly recommend participation in all sectors. With numerous exhibitors and guests from both the region and abroad, this event is fast becoming one of the leading agricultural exhibitions in the region.This year brings the continued success of the Indigenous Cattle Breed Exhibition and Sale, showcasing the finest cattle breeds of Zimbabwe, being the Mashona, Nkone and Tuli breeds. This year promises to be even bigger and better as this standout event, showcasing the best of Zimbabwean agriculture whilst introducing some indigenous small livestock (sheep) to this year’s event and is certainly not to be missed.ART Farm remains committed to its ongoing mission of delivering state-of-the-art research and training, thus equipping Zimbabwean farmers with essential knowledge, practical guidance, and unwavering support. This commitment aligns with the national vision of food security positioning Zimbabwe as the breadbasket of Africa.Intensive research efforts are underway at ART Farm, focusing on pre-release testing of maize and wheat varieties’ resistance to drought, diseases and pests. Additionally, research extends to crops such as soyabean, barley, dry beans, and vegetables where new products including bio-stimulants, pesticides, herbicides, and soil conditioning products are also tested. Furthermore, ART Farm sustains its research activities through the cultivation of commercial crops and the rearing of quality feeder steers, ensuring self-sufficiency and the continuity of vital research operations.In response to climate change and soil rehabilitation needs, we have implemented trials in Regenerative Agriculture, integrating eco-friendly practices across crops and livestock management. Through sustainable land preparation, planting methods, and holistic livestock husbandry techniques we are enhancing soil condition, health and fertility while fostering biodiversity. Our goal is to become a leading hub for regenerative agriculture, offering farmers insights into diverse techniques for achieving optimal outcomes.Our overall goal is to cultivate healthier crops and livestock, thereby ensuring a more wholesome and reliable food supply and a healthier population. This journey towards improved agricultural outcomes is one we are committed to undertaking hand in hand with Zimbabwe’s farmers. We are dedicated to collaborating closely with organizations such as ADMA and stakeholders across the agricultural spectrum.We firmly believe that ART Farm is a significant force in the field of agriculture, serving as a national asset that deserves recognition and reverence in the years to come. Situated near the capital city and at the heart of agricultural activities, its significance cannot be overstated.The Agricultural Research Trust (ART Farm) is unique and without fail, essential to Zimbabwe and the agricultural industry.

As Zimbabwe’s premier agricultural showcase, the ADMA Agrishow will mark another successful event this year, alongside the third Indigenous livestock breeds exhibition and sale.

Still a relatively new addition to the programme, the livestock section has brought fresh energy and depth to the annual event. What began as an addition has quickly become one of the show’s headline attractions, with crowds gathering to witness the excitement of the auction held on the final day.The Agrishow’s first Indigenous cattle sale took place in 2024. Traditionally, the third day of the show on Saturday signalled the winding down of proceedings. The decision to host the auction as the grand finale has proved a masterstroke, revitalising Saturday and transforming it into one of the most anticipated moments of the show.Saturday now belongs to Zimbabwe’s Indigenous Sanga cattle, the Mashona, Nkone/Nguni and Tuli.

2025 sale recapFor the second consecutive year, these locally adapted breeds headlined their own dedicated annual sale under the Zimbabwe National Indigenous Breeds Sale (ZNIBS) banner. It remains the only combined Indigenous breeds sale of its kind in the country.

Under the stewardship of Marco Garizio, chairman of ADMA, and Mark Hook, chairman of the Zimbabwe National Indigenous Breeds Society (ZNIBS), proceedings formally opened before auctioneers Kevin Higgins and Frans Briers took charge.What followed was a spirited contest between online and in-person buyers. The hybrid format broadened participation and amplified competition in the ring. For those yet to experience the theatre of a livestock auction, the far top right corner of the Showgrounds has become essential viewing, a place where anticipation, strategy and split-second decisions converge.Even away from the sale ring, the livestock pens offered plenty to see. Last year, Nguni (also known as Sabi) sheep, Zimbabwe’s Indigenous sheep breed, were showcased in the new small stock holding pens, further expanding the indigenous presence at the show.

Bulls lead the chargeThe sale opened strongly. Lot 1, a bull from Oldonyo Tuli Stud in Tengwe, set the tone at USD 4,750. Despite a handful of Tuli heifers not meeting their reserve prices, firm values were maintained throughout.

Six Tuli studs (Solar, Atwell, Zimbo, Oldonyo, Muteta and Jambo) entered animals.They were followed by Mashona bulls from established names Fertyline, Blue Gums and Zviko, with Machiki of Marondera making an encouraging debut.The Nkone,/Nguni represented by four studs, matched the day’s top price of USD 4,750 through Umvutcha Stud. Umvutcha and Shangani Holistic Nkone joined long-standing contributors Have Hook Nkone and Pungeni Nkone in strengthening breed representation.

The figures confirmed sustained demand, particularly for quality bulls and breeding females, underscoring the growing commercial appeal of well-bred, locally adapted genetics.

A sweet bonus roundPlatinum sponsors Fivet Animal Health injected further excitement with a “buy one, get one free” heifer competition. Successful bidders had their buyer numbers entered into a draw for a bonus heifer per breed, a surprise twist that added extra energy to an already buoyant sale ring.

Historic recognition: The Japie Jackson Memorial TrophyA defining moment of the day was the presentation of the inaugural Dr Japie Jackson Memorial Trophy. Judged by respected South African cattle judge Stefan Buys, the award went to Lot 53, a Blue Gums Mashona Stud heifer bred by Maree Osborne of Macheke.

Crafted by the renowned Patrick Mavros studio, the silver heifer trophy stands on a three-sided base symbolising the Mashona, Nkone and Tuli breeds. It was presented in a poignant ceremony by Laila and Sienna Pole, granddaughters of George Hulme of Pungeni Nkone Stud.The heifer’s buyers (the management team for Edson Maduwara of Farm 215, Ziyambe, Dorowa) described the purchase as a privilege, calling the animal “a shining example of what excellence in Mashona breeding looks like” and celebrating the occasion as a tribute to collaboration, breeding excellence and Japie Jackson’s enduring legacy.

The story behind the trophyThe concept for the Floating Trophy originated from George Hulme’s compilation,The Cattle and Veld Philosophy of Dr Japie Jackson,a collection of Jackson’s writings. Proceeds from the publication were donated to support the promotion of the Zimbabwe National Indigenous Breeds Sale and ultimately funded the trophy, now destined to become a permanent annual feature.

Japie Jackson was a lifelong advocate of Zimbabwe’s indigenous Sanga breeds. He believed in managing cattle and grazing systems as simply and naturally as possible, maximising the inherent strengths of adapted cattle and the resilience of the veld itself.Many individuals contributed to bringing the trophy to life, including Nigel Joscylin, Patrick Mavros Jnr., Fivet Animal Health, Oldonyo Tuli and Mashona studs, Pungeni Nkone, Willie Swan, CC Sales, Have Hook Nkone Stud and numerous others.

Beyond the figures, the 2025 ZNIBS sale reflected a deeper shift. Indigenous breeds are no longer regarded as nostalgic relics but as practical, forward-looking solutions to modern production challenges, offering exceptional heat tolerance, disease resistance, feed efficiency and resilience under drought conditions.

With climate uncertainty intensifying and input costs escalating, Zimbabwe’s Sanga cattle are steadily reclaiming their rightful place at the centre of the national herd.As this year’s ADMA Agrishow unfolds, the message is clear: Zimbabwe’s indigenous cattle are receiving the recognition and the market confidence they have long deserved.

The Zimbabwe Herd Book (ZHB) Beef School returns in September 2026 with a strong, practical programme designed to support livestock producers across the country, this time being hosted in Harare for the first time in many years.

The move to bring the event to our capital city comes at an important time for the agricultural sector. With fuel prices recently rocketing, hosting the Beef School in Harare is expected to significantly improve accessibility, allowing more farmers, students, and industry stakeholders to attend without the burden of long-distance travel costs.This year’s programme features a diverse and highly experienced line-up of local and international speakers, each addressing critical aspects of modern beef and small livestock production.

Beef SchoolDay One (Tuesday 15 September) of the event opens with a session by Catriona Millen from Australia’s Agricultural Business Research Institute (ABRI) on selection in practice, providing insights into how data-driven breeding decisions can improve herd performance. This is followed by Willem Augustyn, who will explore the importance of nutrition on fetal programming and its long-term impact on productivity.

Animal health remains a key priority, with Department of Veterinary Services Chief Director, Dr Pious Makaya delivering a Zimbabwe animal health update, giving farmers a current overview of disease trends and management considerations.The programme also highlights market realities, with Livestock Meat and Advisory Council’s Dr Reneth Mano presenting on meat protein markets, offering perspective on demand trends and positioning for profitability.A major feature of the day will be Dr Jan Myburgh, who will speak on bridging the gap between natural remedies and conventional veterinary medicine, an increasingly relevant topic as farmers seek cost-effective and sustainable health solutions.Genetic progress is further explored by Prof Weaber, who will focus on selecting for maternal performance, while renowned cattle judge PJ Budler will share insights into global stud breeding trends.

The day also aligns with the Beef School’s theme “Year of the Boran,” with contributions from industry experts including Pikkie Uys, reinforcing the breed’s growing importance in regional beef systems.On Day Two (Wednesday 16 September), Dr Danie Odendaal will address farm management planning, while Delwyn Roberts covers feeding for body condition to maximise fertility. Feed and input trends will be unpacked by Dr Chrispen Sukume in his talk on raw materials and feed trends. From a financial perspective, Rowan Hayter will guide farmers through cash flow management in beef cattle, helping producers navigate economic pressures.

The programme for both cattle and small-stock producers also includes practical demonstrations and solutions from industry players such as:

* Lozino / Red Dane Agri Solutions (knapsack and spray race systems)* Nemtech (electric fencing and handling facilities)* Trouw (home feed mixing solutions).

Additional sessions include labour motivation by Ajs Kirk and fixed-time artificial insemination (AI) by ZHB Chair Anne Cooke.

That evening, the Beef School will acknowledge effort and excellence within the livestock sector with the ZHB Awards.

Small-stock SchoolThe third day of the event (Thursday 17 September) broadens the focus to small-stock management, offering practical, hands-on knowledge key to improving productivity in small-stock enterprises.

Practical insights will come from Delwyn Roberts on sheep feeding and valuable insights into practical animal health from Dr Danie Odendaal.

Selection and breeding are again emphasised, with Dorper Society Chairman William Hundermark presenting on practical sheep selection, alongside a session on artificial insemination in sheep by Pikkie Uys, while Dr Jesse Steele focuses on wireworm challenges in sheep, a critical issue for flock health.

An exciting addition to the event is sure to be the sheepdog demonstration by William Hundermark, ensuring a well-rounded, applied learning experience.Organisers emphasise that hosting the event in Harare is a deliberate step toward inclusivity during a time of rising operational costs.By reducing travel barriers, the 2026 Beef School aims to ensure that knowledge-sharing, innovation, and collaboration remain accessible to the widest possible audience at a time when informed decision-making is more important than ever.As Zimbabwe’s livestock sector continues to adapt to economic and environmental pressures, the ZHB Beef School remains a key platform for equipping farmers with practical tools, current insights, and valuable industry connections.

George Hulme of Pungeni Nkone stud speaks with the clarity of someone who has spent decades observing cattle navigate the unforgiving landscape of Zimbabwe. His words carry a weight that transcends mere breeding philosophy: “Let us not forget that our indigenous cattle are functional efficient breeds and the pretty colours of the Nkone, as an example, and any other cosmetic traits, are not terribly important. We should all be more concerned about efficient production from our Sanga indigenous breeds rather than cosmetic attributes, to ensure their future as important breeds or ecotypes.Form always follows Function.”

This statement represents more than breeding preferences. It embodies a fundamental understanding of what Zimbabwe needs from its cattle, what the land demands, and what the future of sustainable livestock production requires in a region where climate uncertainty and resource scarcity are becoming the norm rather than the exception.

Understanding the SangaZimbabwe’s three breeds of indigenous cattle are part of the Sanga group, a distinctive type of African cattle characterised by their adaptation to harsh environmental conditions. Unlike the heavily dependent breeds of temperate regions, Sanga cattle evolved through centuries of natural selection in Africa’s harsh environments that would destroy lesser animals. The Zimbabwean Sanga specifically developed in harsh regions of Zimbabwe and neighbouring areas, shaped by drought, disease, poor forage, and the practical needs of pastoral communities.

Hulme emphasises the breed’s environmental versatility: “The Sanga excels on all veld and soil types and thrives on poor soil and veld, from the very hot, drought-prone, low-altitude sweetveld areas to the high-rainfall, highveld sourveld.”These cattle carry the genetic legacy of survival. Their ancestors were those that could walk long distances to water, those that could maintain body condition on sparse grazing, those that resisted tick-borne diseases that decimated imported breeds, and those that could reproduce reliably year after year without intensive management.To understand Hulme’s emphasis on function, one must first understand the environment these cattle must navigate. Zimbabwe’s environment is largely characterised by erratic rainfall patterns that have become increasingly unpredictable. “ART is not only set up to serve farmers but is also set up by farmers and managed by farmers,” Winkfield said. “That means the ideas for our research come straight from the source. Above the mud as drones enter the conversationWhile the field plots grounded the day in agronomy, discussion among speakers increasingly turned to the role of drone technology in crop protection.

Dr Dumisani Kutwayo, Chief Director in the Department of Research and Specialist Services (above with an exhibitor),said the increased use of drones this season has been driven largely by weather conditions.“Most of us noticed that this year it was very difficult to spray using tractor or knapsack sprayers because of the heavy rains,” Kutwayo said. “As a result, there was an increase in the use of drones.”However, he cautioned that current agrochemical labels do not yet accommodate this method of application.“If you look at our pesticide labels, you won’t find any recommendations for drones,” Kutwayo said. “Yet they are being used.”Kutwayo explained that the Ministry has responded by establishing a Technical Subcommittee on drone use in agriculture, bringing together stakeholders from CropLife, universities, drone operators and the Civil Aviation Authority of Zimbabwe.“In order to develop standard operating procedures, we have also developed a questionnaire that will be administered to farmers and applicators,” Kutwayo said. “This is so that the SOPs are informed by real experience on the ground.”He added that the intention is to “safeguard the farmer, the consumer and the environment.”

A regulatory grey zoneGeoff Bradshaw, a consultant and trainer in chemical application who sits on the Ministry’s subcommittee, said the absence of label guidance creates a clear compliance issue.

“It is technically illegal to apply products using equipment that is not specified on the label,” Bradshaw said. “And that includes drones.”Bradshaw noted that this has implications for liability, insurance and export compliance, particularly where Good Agricultural Practice (GAP) and maximum residue level (MRL) standards must be met.He also stressed that the role of drones extends beyond spraying.“Drones can be used for scouting, identifying stress in crops, and pinpointing problem areas,” Bradshaw said. “The potential is enormous, but we are well behind in putting the proper frameworks in place.”

“The committee was only set up recently, but we are working towards putting proper procedures in place,” he said.Bradshaw added that Zimbabwe is playing catch-up compared to other regions.“In countries like Japan, they’ve had procedures in place for decades,” he said. “We’ve got a long way to go, but we are on the way.”

FAMS Freight Forwarding (Pvt) Ltd is a Zimbabwean-based customs clearing agent and the exclusive representative of DSV - one of the world’s leading logistics and freight forwarding companies. Over the years, we have positioned ourselves as the trusted logistics partner for farmers and agribusinesses.

Agriculture remains the backbone of Zimbabwe’s economy, employing much of the population and contributing significantly to exports such as tobacco, maize, cotton, and horticultural products. With our experience, FAMS bridges the gap between Zimbabwe’s agricultural potential and global market access.

Blocking the Hormuz Corridor and what that means for Agricultural logisticsThe Strait of Hormuz is a critical maritime chokepoint through which a significant share of fertilizer inputs pass. Much of this fertilizer is received by sub-Saharan Africa, with Zimbabwe specifically importing US$388 million worth of fertilizers in 2023. This is used to prop up the country’s vital agricultural sector.

The ongoing blockade of the Hormuz Corridor has thusly impacted agricultural businesses in Zimbabwe greatly. The UN Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD) notes that shipping through the Hormuz Corridor has fallen by 95%, and Chief Economist of the Food & Agriculture Organisation (FAO), Máximo Torero, has warned that “Between 20% and 30% of global fertilizer exports are not moving out.”This drop in supply has raised prices of fertilizer by 27% to 40% according to a report by the Global Sovereign Advisory (GSA). Alongside that, the blockade has pushed up fuel prices, increasing transport costs of moving crops and agricultural equipment across Zimbabwe. These costs pass on to the prices of grown crops, such as rice and wheat, both imported and locally grown. All this ultimately results in a severe strain on the country’s economy and food supply.

The FAMS solutionWe at FAMS - Freight & Management Solutions are no strangers to tough logistics problems. As our name states, we take pride in our ability to provide good solutions for our client’s logistics needs, no matter the situation. In the case of the disruption to the Hormuz Corridor, we have identified that the most important goals are to reduce costs and keep the flow of imports clear and efficient.

To this end, we have invested in temperature-controlled transport with consistent tracking and monitoring of cargo – ensuring that agricultural perishables stay fresh as long as possible, with clients always aware of their products status. Our bonded warehouses in Harare and Bulawayo provide secure storage, distribution, and consolidation services – providing security to clients during this tumultuous time. We maintain expertise with customs clearance and compliance, always staying on top of the regulatory changes the blockade causes. In this way we keep the import of fertilizer, equipment, and other agricultural goods clear and efficient, preventing hold ups at customs. Most importantly, our dedicated team of logistics professionals plan and co-ordinate shipping carefully, making sure clients are advised on the current best routes and are also aware of the current risks.

Why Use FAMS?Our expertiseWe define cargo types (bulk, containerized, perishable, hazardous), volume, frequency, origins and destinations of shipments and quote accordingly. We advise on the right mode and size of containers to use. We Identify whether you require specialized services (cold chain, hazardous goods, express delivery). We offer value-added services like customs clearance, warehousing (bonded and general), and license and permit applications.

Customers need to look beyond price and evaluate service quality, delivery times, and customer support. There are hidden costs in logistics, compliance, and international regulations which, as experts, we are aware of and communicate these to the customers to avoid delays and storage bills.

Our reliabilityMany of our long-term customers, some of whom we have serviced for over 20 years, credit us with exceptional service delivery. As FAMS, we have come to understand that strong relationships often lead to priority service and better terms which we in turn pass on to our customer. We offer internationally recognized insurance coverage for goods in transit, and we have adopted tracking systems for real-time visibility.

We have been nominated agency of the year twice- an award voted for by other agents in the country; however, our employees remain the integral part of our service delivery and excellence!Always remember, cheapest isn’t always best—late deliveries or damaged goods cost more long-term. Look for providers with global networks and local presence in your target markets.

AZimbabwean-manufactured, towable solar power unit which made its debut at the ZWE Steel stand at the Agrishow last year, is now being sold as an off-grid electricity solution for farms struggling under decades of unreliable grid supply.

For Zimbabwean commercial farmers, electricity is a production input as critical as seed or fertiliser. Irrigation pivots, grain handling equipment, cold storage, and workshop tools all depend on power that, for much of the past two decades, the national grid has failed to reliably supply. Load-shedding schedules of twelve hours or more per day remain common in rural areas, and the cost of diesel-powered generation has risen sharply alongside global fuel prices.It is against that backdrop that ZWE Steel and Romtech Solutions have introduced the VoltWagon: a mobile, trailer-mounted solar power system aimed at agricultural and industrial users who need electricity in locations where the grid either does not reach or cannot be trusted.The VoltWagon is, in essence, a solar-powered inverter system on wheels. The unit carries four 595-watt solar panels, giving a combined peak generation capacity of 2,380 watts, together with three 3 kVA Victron inverters and two BYD 5 kWh lithium-ion batteries. Total usable battery storage in the standard configuration is therefore 10 kWh, though the manufacturers note that battery capacity can be customised to client specifications.The system provides a full 400-volt, three-phase output as well as single-phase supply, making it compatible with larger three-phase agricultural motors, including those used on centre-pivot irrigation systems. A generator plug-in port allows an external petrol or diesel generator to supplement charging on overcast days, a practical acknowledgement that solar generation in Zimbabwe, while generally strong, is not guaranteed year-round.The trailer structure is manufactured from steel and is rated for towing on farm roads at speeds up to 15 km/h. Safety features include temperature-controlled ventilation fans, fire containment enclosures around the battery bank and inverter bay, and a bypass switch in the event of system failure. A Victron Ekrano GX device provides onboard monitoring, while a GPS tracker allows remote location of the unit, a relevant feature given the security environment on Zimbabwean farms.

Pivot performanceThe manufacturers share two specific performance figures for centre-pivot irrigation use. A 20-hectare pivot operating at 20 percent of full speed will run for approximately 30 hours on battery alone, with no solar input. The same pivot running at full capacity draws down the battery in approximately six hours without solar contribution. When solar panels are generating, they can simultaneously power the pivot and recharge the batteries, the critical qualifier being that this is only possible during daylight hours and under adequate irradiance.

These figures give farmers a working basis for planning. A pivot running through the night at reduced speed could, in principle, complete a meaningful irrigation cycle on stored energy before solar generation resumes at dawn. At full speed, the stored capacity is insufficient for overnight-only operation, and either a generator supplement or grid top-up would be required for extended uninterrupted runs.At full pivot speed and no solar input, six hours of battery runtime places the VoltWagon in the category of a supplement to existing power sources rather than a complete replacement.

The generator comparisonOn running costs, a solar unit with no fuel requirement offers a structural advantage over any generator over its operational life, provided the capital cost can be recovered within a reasonable period. According to the manufacturer, generator lifespans typically run five to ten years, against a stated ten to twenty-plus years for the VoltWagon, though battery replacement costs would need to be factored into any honest long-term cost calculation.

In Zimbabwe, fuel shortages have historically disrupted farming operations at critical points in the agricultural calendar. A solar-battery system eliminates fuel supply as a risk variable entirely but a startup cost comparison favours generators as the VoltWagon represents a higher initial investment. For farmers whose capital is constrained, and many Zimbabwean farmers are operating in exactly that environment, this remains a practical barrier.

Monitoring and connectivityThe remote monitoring capability, delivered through the Victron Ekrano GX platform, allows operators to view real-time data on battery state of charge, solar generation output, AC load consumption, and system voltage and temperature. Published data shows consumption of 3.7 kWh and solar generation of 5.9 kWh over a two-day window, figures consistent with modest agricultural or small-industrial loads during daylight hours.

GPS tracking is included as standard. In a country where farm equipment theft is an ongoing concern, this feature has operational value beyond simple asset management.

Manufactured in ZimbabweThe VoltWagon is a joint product of ZWE Steel, which handles the structural fabrication, and Romtech Solutions, which integrates the electrical systems. Both are Zimbabwean companies. The inverters are sourced from Victron Energy, a Dutch manufacturer widely used in the Southern African off-grid solar market, and the batteries are BYD units, a Chinese manufacturer with a substantial global presence in stationary storage.

The concept is sound - the VoltWagon addresses a genuine and persistent problem. Zimbabwe’s commercial farming sector has been managing power unreliability for long enough that a mobile, off-grid solar unit with three-phase output capability fills a recognisable gap. The use of established components (Victron inverters, BYD batteries) rather than unknown-brand alternatives is a point in its favour.As with any solar-battery system, performance is tied to weather, which in Zimbabwe’s wet season can mean extended cloud cover at precisely the time when irrigation and post-harvest handling demands are highest.For farmers who have already invested in solar infrastructure and are looking for a portable supplement, or for those evaluating alternatives to generator fleets, the VoltWagon warrants a detailed quotation and a site-specific load analysis before any purchase decision.

Paul Christopher Alfred Johnson, known to many simply as Chris, leaves behind an enduring legacy in Zimbabwe’s cattle industry, built on more than five decades of dedication to the Tuli breed.

Born in Harare on 24 August 1936, Chris grew up on family farms in Macheke and Marondera, laying out the foundation for a lifelong commitment to agriculture. He was educated at Plumtree School before attending Gwebi Agricultural College (1956–1958), where he excelled academically, earning a First-Class Diploma with distinctions in both Field and Animal Husbandry. His performance at Gwebi marked him early as a farmer of exceptional ability and discipline.After gaining practical experience in Goromonzi and at Horseshoe Block, Chris established himself in Tengwe in the mid-1960s on Jambo Farm. Like many pioneer farmers of that era, development began from the ground up, prioritising infrastructure, water security, and land preparation under challenging conditions.It was here that Chris would make his most significant and lasting contribution to Zimbabwean agriculture.Following the lifting of restrictions on cattle in the Tengwe area in 1968, Chris began building what would become the renowned Jambo Tuli Stud. Over the next 50-plus years, he developed one of the most respected and influential Tuli herds in the country. Today, Jambo is recognised as the longest-running Tuli stud in Zimbabwe, with its genetics represented widely across herds both locally and regionally.Chris’s approach to cattle breeding was defined by discipline, attention to detail, and an uncompromising pursuit of quality. He maintained meticulous handwritten records, with an exceptional ability to recall bloodlines, performance traits, and individual animal histories. His deep understanding of the breed allowed him to make consistent, long-term genetic improvements, contributing significantly to the strength and adaptability of Tuli cattle in Zimbabwe.Beyond his own herd, Chris played an important role within the wider cattle breeding community. He was a longstanding member of the Tuli Society for nearly six decades, where his steady, thoughtful input earned him widespread respect. Known for his measured and practical perspective, he provided guidance that balanced innovation with proven principles, a voice of experience that helped shape decision-making within the breed.Chris was also a mentor to many emerging farmers and breeders. He gave generously of his time and knowledge, guiding others through breeding decisions and encouraging a deeper understanding of the Tuli breed. His willingness to support younger farmers ensured that his influence extended far beyond his own operation.Over time, Chris expanded his farming enterprise, acquiring additional properties to support the growth of his herd to a significant scale. However, it was not size alone that defined his success, but the consistency and quality of the cattle he produced.Today, Chris’s legacy continues strongly under the leadership of his son, Oscar Johnson, who is carrying forward the Jambo Tuli Stud with the same commitment to quality, integrity, and breed excellence. The continuity of this family operation stands as a testament to the solid foundation Chris established over decades.In recognition of this enduring legacy, Jambo Tuli animals will be featured at the ADMA Agrishow’s third Indigenous Breed Sale, offering breeders the opportunity to access genetics shaped by generations of careful selection and dedication.

Those who worked alongside Chris will remember his quiet confidence, integrity, and unwavering standards. He was not a man of unnecessary words, but when he spoke, his insights carried weight. His legacy is reflected not only in the cattle he bred, but in the many breeders he influenced and the enduring strength of the Tuli breed in Zimbabwe today.

Chris Johnson’s contribution to agriculture, and particularly to the development of the Tuli breed, will continue to be felt for generations to come.

Our journey with Mashona cattle began in 1997, when my husband John and I acquired a cancelled export consignment of 30 heifers, born in 1995, along with a bull. These animals came from Fertyline Mashona, bred by the late Carmen Stubbs, a respected Mashona breeder from Headlands in Manicaland, not far from where we farm today.

We had purchased our farm in 1989, at a time when there were no cattle on the property. My own livestock experience was limited and gradual, starting with goats in 1987 and later moving on to sheep. Originally from Melbourne, Australia, my professional background was in education, not agriculture. Cattle farming, and particularly indigenous cattle, became a journey of learning by doing.Over the years, we developed a structured paddock system aligned with our cropping programme. Detailed records were introduced and carefully maintained, and slowly the herd grew. In the early days, tick control involved knapsack spraying and the manual application of tick grease. As the incidence of theileriosis (East Coast Fever) increased, we installed a fixed spray race. More recently, we invested in a portable race system, allowing us to take handling facilities directly to the cattle. This significantly reduces the time animals spend away from grazing.

Systemic acaricides are now applied as a pour-on, with problem ticks hand-dressed when necessary. The difference in efficiency is remarkable: the process is quicker, calmer, and far less stressful for the cattle. The portable races are also fast to erect and move, making them a practical addition to our management system.

An interesting observation on our farm has been the relationship between wildlife and tick control. As our guineafowl population has increased, tick pressure has noticeably declined.During the dry season, supplementary feeding consists mainly of crop residues and molasses, while mineral supplementation is provided in summer.

In its early years, the Society worked to protect the purity of Mashona cattle at a time when national policy favoured diluting communal herds with exotic genetics. This group played a crucial role in safeguarding Zimbabwe’s indigenous cattle heritage.

We recently experienced losses due to hyena attacks, resulting in injuries and two deaths. Exposure to all facets of beef production accelerated my learning curve dramatically.Successful breeding, in my experience, comes down to passion, attention to detail, continuous staff training and empowering people to understand not just how things are done, but why.

Promoting indigenous breeds2026 marks the third year of the Indigenous Cattle Sale held at the annual ADMA (Agricultural Dealers and Manufacturers Association) Agrishow. This initiative has played an important role in promoting Mashona, Nkone and Tuli cattle. Last year saw the introduction of the Dr Japie Jackson Memorial Trophy for the best female animal on show, an honour I was privileged to receive as the inaugural winner.

This recognition opened the door to the Champion of the World Cattle Photo Competition, organised by international cattle judge PJ Budler. We entered a top bull named Mambo, meaning ‘Chief’ in Shona, and he placed third in the “Other Breeds” category.

The Mashona cow is highly sought after, but it is essential to maintain a nucleus herd to keep producing purebred females and this requires a Mashona bull.Mashona bulls are particularly effective for reducing cow size. Smaller cows require less feed to resume cycling, while larger cows need more resources before reaching the same point. The mathematics are simple.

Introducing new geneticsLast year, we introduced Mashona genetics from the United States. In the early 1990s, Jim Weaver was working in Zimbabwe and observed indigenous cattle thriving despite minimal winter feed, then flourishing in summer. Determined to introduce these genetics to Texas, five breeders supplied cows to Dr Percy Sharp, who produced embryos that formed the foundation of Mashona cattle in the USA.

Our semen straws were sourced from Dr Bill Satterfield of Dry Creek Livestock in Elgin, Texas. As there is currently no governing body for Mashona cattle in the USA, the semen is registered as Appendix A. The resulting progeny are showing encouraging potential.

Grass, management and sustainabilityMy passion for Mashona cattle has led me on an extraordinary journey and one that has also become a viable business. Now retired from crop farming, the cattle contribute meaningfully to our financial security.

We consider ourselves grass farmers first and foremost. Grass production is closely monitored, and every usable area is optimised. Recently, solar-powered electric fencing has been brought back into use, proving invaluable for managing small grazing blocks.Lantana, a rapidly spreading noxious weed, demands constant vigilance. Initially removed using a tractor and chain, we now rely on targeted spot-spraying with specialised herbicides during flowering, using a custom-built motorised sprayer.The mobile race system has further improved efficiency. Reducing walking time to the dip by several hours means more time (up to three hours) grazing, and contented cows. Condition scoring has replaced frequent weighing, saving time while providing a more meaningful assessment of animal performance.

Winter is often viewed as a quieter period for cattle health because tick numbers may appear lower than they are during the rainy season. However, this perception can be misleading. For cattle producers, winter dipping remains a critical disease-prevention practice, particularly in the control of January Disease, also known astheileriosis.

January Disease is caused by the blood parasiteTheileria parvaand is transmitted mainly by brown ear ticks. The disease can cause severe losses when tick control is inconsistent, when there is uncontrolled movement of cattle, or when farmers only respond after animals begin to show clinical signs. By that stage, infection pressure may already be high within the herd and the surrounding environment.

Why the brown ear tick mattersThe brown ear tick is especially important because it is a three-host tick. This means it requires three separate hosts to complete its life cycle. Like other ticks, it develops from egg to larva, then nymph, and finally adult. Each active stage feeds on an animal before dropping back to the ground and moulting into the next stage.Figure 1: Three-host tick life cycle: larva, nymph and adult stages feed on different hosts before dropping off to moult or lay eggs.In practical terms, the larva hatches from eggs on the ground, finds a host, feeds, then drops off and moults into a nymph. The nymph repeats the process and later moults into an adult. Adult ticks then attach to another host, feed, mate, and the female drops off to lay eggs on the ground. The cycle then starts again.

This life cycle is central to the spread of January Disease. A tick can pick upTheileria parvawhile feeding on an infected animal during one life stage, such as the larval or nymphal stage. After moulting, it can transmit the parasite to another animal during the next stage. This process is called trans-stadial transmission. It allows infection to be carried from one tick stage to the next, making the brown ear tick an efficient vector.

Why winter dipping should not be relaxedMany farmers associate ticks with the wet season, but the risk of January Disease does not disappear during winter. Immature tick stages can survive during parts of the dry season, and brown ear ticks can maintain the disease cycle even when visible tick burdens appear low. Missing dips during winter allows ticks and infection pressure to build up quietly. When warmer and wetter conditions return, the herd may face a much higher disease challenge.

Historically, January Disease was associated with certain areas and seasons because different brown ear tick species are adapted to different environments.Rhipicephalus appendiculatus(more common) is commonly associated with warmer, moister highveld conditions, whileRhipicephalus zambeziensisis better adapted to hotter and drier lowveld environments. These ecological differences have influenced when and where disease risk is greatest.However, the current situation is more complex. Cattle movement, changes in grazing patterns, inconsistent dipping, and movement of animals between ecological zones can introduce infected cattle and ticks into new areas. Once established, these ticks may continue the transmission cycle. Farmers should therefore avoid assuming that January Disease is only a rainy-season problem or only a problem in traditionally known risk areas.

What farmers should doThe most important message is simple: do not stop dipping in winter. Dipping should remain consistent and should follow veterinary recommendations for the area. Where weekly dipping is advised, farmers should maintain that interval so that the dipping cycle is not broken.

Farmers should also pay attention to dip management. The correct dip concentration must be used, animals must be fully and properly dipped, and dip tanks should be maintained so that the chemical remains effective. Poor mixing, under-strength dip, irregular dipping, or failure to dip all animals can allow ticks to survive and continue spreading disease.Regular inspection is also important. Farmers should check animals frequently and report unusual illness early, especially fever, swollen lymph nodes, weakness, loss of appetite, difficult breathing, or sudden deaths.Animal movement must also be controlled. Illegal or uncontrolled movement of cattle can spread infected ticks and carrier animals into new areas. Newly purchased or moved animals should be inspected, treated where necessary, and kept separate before being mixed with the main herd. Farmers should always follow local veterinary movement regulations.

The take-home messageWinter dipping should not be treated as a routine activity that only matters when ticks are visible. It is a critical disease-prevention measure that helps break the January Disease transmission cycle before it becomes a major herd problem. The brown ear tick’s three-host life cycle allows it to acquireTheileria parvafrom one animal and transmit it to another at a later stage, which makes consistent tick control essential.

By maintaining regular winter dipping, using the correct dip concentration, monitoring animals closely, and controlling cattle movement, farmers can reduce the risk of January Disease, protect herd health, and prevent avoidable mortalities. Good winter tick control prepares cattle for healthier, stronger and more productive performance when the rains return.

Point to note:Ticks may look fewer in winter, but the disease risk remains. Consistent dipping protects the herd before visible problems appear.

Zimbabwe’s indigenous goat breeds, the Matabele and Mashona, represent centuries of natural selection and adaptation to our unique environment. Yet despite their remarkable resilience, disease resistance, and proven ability to thrive under harsh conditions, these hardy breeds remain largely undervalued in our small-stock industry. As commercial farmers increasingly turn to exotic breeds, we risk losing the genetic wealth embedded in our local goats, animals that have sustained rural communities for generations without expensive inputs or intensive management.

This article explores the distinctive characteristics that make our indigenous goats uniquely suited to Zimbabwe’s climate and farming systems, examines the breed standards that define the Matabele and Mashona, and outlines practical strategies for conserving and improving these invaluable genetic resources. Understanding what makes these breeds exceptional is the first step toward unlocking their economic potential and ensuring a sustainable future for goat farming across our nation.

The Matabele goat: built for ZimbabweThe Matabele goat, called Nguni or Ndebele in different regions, thrives in the drier parts of Zimbabwe, from Matabeleland North and South into sections of Midlands province. These medium to large animals, brought by Bantu tribes from the North, have spent centuries becoming perfectly suited to our climate.

At 65 centimetres tall at the withers, Matabele goats come in every shade you can imagine: white, black, brown, cream, and countless mixed patterns. Long, pendulous ears with turned-up tips give them their distinctive look, and many carry the traditional tassels or wattles under the neck that farmers associate with fertility.The numbers tell the real story. At a mature weight of 45 kilograms, these goats produce twins 62% of the time and triplets 1.6% of the time. With a prolificacy rate of 1.7 and a weaning rate of 119%, they outperform many exotic breeds costing ten times as much. They kid year-round, with 60% of births happening during the dry season when feed is scarcest. Try getting that from a pampered exotic breed.

The Mashona goat: Compact and resilientMashona goats take a different approach. Small and compact at 50 centimetres at the withers, these hardy animals carry short ears held horizontally and, in males, a dramatic mane running the full length of the back. Both sexes grow scimitar-shaped horns, erect and heavy at the base, ranging from 2.5 to 20 centimetres.Like Matabeles, Mashona goats often have the valued toggles or wattles. Their faces frequently show distinctive V-shaped markings between the eyes stretching to the nose, in combinations of black, white, and brown that correspond to body colouring. These patterns often indicate specific ecotypes adapted to particular environments.Why standards matterBreed standards exist for practical reasons, not aesthetics. Fertility and hardiness drive these requirements, and they translate directly into profit. Strong, straight legs allow goats to rear up and browse high branches when ground vegetation disappears. Well-developed udders with prominent teats mean kids that grow fast. Balanced, healthy testes in bucks ensure good breeding rates.Serious defects should get culled immediately. Bowed legs and knock knees are highly heritable and compromise mobility. Split scrotums affect fertility. Animals failing these standards should leave the breeding pool to keep the genetics clean.The problemUncontrolled crossbreeding is destroying these breeds. As Boer and Kalahari genes spread through indigenous flocks, centuries of local adaptation disappear. Without inspection systems and enforcement, farmers have no guidance on what to keep and what to cull. The genetic erosion happens quietly, one breeding season at a time.What we have to work withThe infrastructure exists. Research institutions and universities have collected substantial data on both breeds. Large populations remain available for selection work. The Goat Breeders Association of Zimbabwe (GBAZ) provides organisational structure. The Zimbabwe Herd Book (ZHB) offers registration systems.

The missing piece is human capital. Without trained, registered inspectors who understand these breeds thoroughly, all that infrastructure sits idle. We need people who can walk through a herd, evaluate animals against proper standards, and guide breeding decisions.

Moving forwardZimbabwe’s small-stock industry can’t fulfil its potential while ignoring animals proven in local conditions. Matabele and Mashona goats don’t just survive where exotic breeds struggle, they produce consistently, breed reliably, and require minimal intervention. They kid when feed is scarce, browse at heights other goats can’t reach, and maintain productivity without constant management.

The industry needs formal breeding programs, clear inspection protocols, and trained inspectors who know these animals inside out. These indigenous goats carry adaptive genetics that become more valuable as climate patterns shift and farming becomes less predictable.Everything needed for success exists: the animals, the data, the organisational structure. What’s been missing is commitment. Will Zimbabwe finally back its indigenous goat breeds with the same resources given to imported genetics?Joseph Sikosana presented this material at the ZHB’s inaugural Small-stock School in Bulawayo in September, highlighting the urgent need for formal recognition and support systems for Zimbabwe’s indigenous goat breeds.

Sikosana (pictured above with ZHB’s Dr Mario Beffa)Joseph Sikosana joined the Department of Research and Specialist Services (DRSS) in 1985 as a Research Officer at Matopos Research Institute, and rose through the ranks, becoming Head of institute in 2003, up to 2009. Thereafter he became Director of Livestock of Livestock and Pastures Research. His research work was mainly based on indigenous goat production. Mr Sikosana retired from service in 2018 and since then, has been involved as a consultant in indigenous goat production.

Individual farmers face prohibitive setup costs for nurseries, covering seedlings, land preparation, fencing, labour, and ongoing management, with no reliable financial support mechanism in place.

Recognising the threat to long-term production sustainability, the Zimbabwean government introduced an afforestation levy in 2015. Set at 0.75% of the gross value of tobacco sales, the levy has generated an estimated USD 50 million over its first decade. The global regulatory tightening: What Zimbabwe must prepare for

The urgency of Zimbabwe’s forestry challenge is amplified significantly by an accelerating wave of international sustainability regulation, much of it directly relevant to tobacco’s key export markets.

European Union

The EU Deforestation Regulation (EUDR) requires that commodities placed on the EU market not originate from land deforested or degraded after 31 December 2020. While tobacco is not currently among the seven listed commodities, the list is explicitly subject to periodic review. Companies trading with the EU must conduct regular supply chain due diligence to ensure compliance. Implementation deadlines are set for December 2026 for large businesses and June 2027 for micro and small enterprises.

Alongside the EUDR, the EU’s Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD) and the Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive (CS3D) further tighten requirements. CS3D establishes a corporate due diligence duty for in-scope companies to identify and address adverse human rights and environmental impacts across their entire value chains, including those of business partners. China

China, Zimbabwe’s single largest tobacco export market at 69% of exports, is moving aggressively on sustainability. In 2024, China announced mandatory Corporate Sustainability Disclosure Standards (CSDS), a unified framework for sustainability performance reporting aligned to global benchmarks including the EU’s CSRD, while in some respects exceeding them in rigor. United States of America

A proposed US Forest Bill (2023) targets products produced on illegally deforested land, requiring importers to certify that affected commodities are free from illegal deforestation. The bill remains at committee stage, and the trajectory of US environmental regulation under the Trump administration remains uncertain. Nonetheless, a December 2024 policy framework aimed at reducing US imports of deforestation-linked products signalled an underlying institutional direction that may prove durable.

International legal obligations

A July 2025 International Court of Justice advisory opinion established that states have binding obligations under international law to take ambitious action against climate change - obligations that implicitly cover deforestation. The Inter-American Court of Human Rights has separately declared a climate emergency, affirming that protecting ecosystems, specifically forests, is crucial to mitigating climate change and ensuring the right to a healthy environment. States are required to adopt measures reflecting the “highest possible ambition” to mitigate climate effects.

These are not aspirational targets; they are procurement requirements with real commercial consequences.

The commercial stakes of market exclusion and the cost of inaction

The regulatory and commercial environment creates three distinct and escalating risks for Zimbabwe’s tobacco sector.

The first is market exclusion. There is a significant and growing risk that foreign customers will “de-risk” by terminating sourcing relationships with suppliers in countries where environmental impacts are difficult to monitor or remain unresolved. Given that 98% of Zimbabwe’s tobacco is exported, even a partial withdrawal by key buyers would be economically devastating.The second is a contractual cascade. Zimbabwe’s 2026 tobacco marketing season is unfolding with sharply contrasting signals; record early volumes on the one hand, and mounting concern from growers on the other, as prices come under pressure in what industry leaders are increasingly describing as an oversupplied market.

Latest figures from the Tobacco Industry and Marketing Board show that by late April, 155.1 million kg of tobacco had been sold, a 56% increase on the same period last year, while earnings have risen 21% to USD 410.3 million. However, the average price remains under pressure at USD 2.65/kg, down from USD 3.41/kg last year (TIMB Weekly Bulletin No.17, 24 April 2026).That disconnect between volume and value is being felt acutely at farm level.In a communication to member producers in April, Zimbabwe Tobacco Association (ZTA) president Graham Ross said the season was progressing with “very mixed feelings on the market and indeed the bottom line,” noting that while some growers have already completed selling, others have yet to begin grading, raising questions about timing strategies and eventual profitability.Ross cautioned that the industry is facing a “local, regional and world oversupply situation,” warning that growers “cannot give any excuse for a price reduction for factors that are in our control”. His remarks come as market data shows quality is a key determinant this season, with lower-grade tobacco dominating deliveries so far.According to industry figures, lower stalk tobacco now accounts for around 62% of deliveries, reflecting a continued skew toward lower-value leaf. Overall market averages sit at approximately USD 2.64/kg, with auction tobacco averaging closer to USD 2.04/kg and contract tobacco around USD 2.32/kg. Higher-value upper stalk tobacco continues to achieve significantly stronger prices, averaging around USD 3.76/kg.This quality skew helps explain the downward pressure on prices despite strong export demand and rising volumes.Ross urged growers to refocus on fundamentals ahead of the next season, highlighting that profitability ultimately rests on three pillars: cost of production, yield, and quality. “Less done properly results in more overall,” he said, cautioning against expanding hectarage as a reaction to tight cashflows.He also warned that rising input costs, particularly fuel, could reshape production decisions, noting that diesel-powered irrigation may become “an absolute non-starter” under current pricing conditions.Despite the challenges, Ross stopped short of writing off the sector, instead framing the outlook in pragmatic terms: “If there is a future, then each grower must ensure that he or she is not bowled out prematurely”.With contract sales continuing to dominate the marketing system and buyers holding significant leverage, the remainder of the season will likely hinge on whether later, higher-quality tobacco can lift average prices, or whether the current trend of high volumes and subdued earnings will define the 2026 crop.The International Tobacco Growers Association (ITGA), an association representing the interests of tobacco farmers globally (and of which the ZTA is one of the founding members), shared context.

Global market context and trendsLeading international leaf merchants have, in recent years, consistently reported low levels of uncommitted stocks, which supported stronger buying activity and encouraged growers globally to expand production.

That cycle is now reversing into oversupply. Recent industry guidance highlights this shift:Alliance One International notes that “continued strong production is expected to result in oversupply levels.”Universal Corporation reports that “flue-cured, burley, and oriental tobacco [have] moved into oversupply positions.”This reflects a broader structural dynamic. As highlighted by the President of the International Tobacco Growers’ Association, José Aranda:

“From a production standpoint, it is very important for each country to be very cautious when planning its production volume, since the aggregate of all these volumes affects global supply and available stocks, and consequently the market prices of the product.”

At a global level, leaf production has expanded sharply, with estimates indicating roughly 25% growth between 2022 and 2025, driven by acreage expansion and recovery from earlier supply constraints.

Current flue-cured Virginia (FCV) forecasts suggest production is stabilising at high levels, with global output projected at approximately 4.2–4.3 billion kg, or around 2.2–2.3 billion kg excluding China - effectively in line with last season, but still elevated relative to historical norms.Major producing countries - and key competitors to Zimbabwe - have also increased output significantly, including Brazil, reinforcing the global supply surge and intensifying competition in export markets.On the demand side, end-product consumption remains relatively flat overall:Global nicotine consumption is broadly stable in volume terms.Cigarettes continue to dominate demand, accounting for the overwhelming majority of usage.Alternative nicotine products are growing, but not yet at a scale sufficient to dictate leaf sales swings.As a result, pricing has stabilised - and in many cases declined - over the past season and into the current one, reflecting the combined effect of replenished stocks, higher production, and steady (but not expanding) demand.This global backdrop is reinforcing downward pressure on leaf prices, placing greater emphasis on quality, efficiency, and disciplined production planning at grower level.

technology inspired by thunderstorms is challenging agriculture’s century-old dependence on synthetic nitrogen and farms around the world, including the ADMA Agrishow venue, ART FARM, right here in Pomona, who are putting it to the test.

Every time a bolt of lightning strikes during a storm, something extraordinary happens in the sky. The colossal energy of the strike tears apart atmospheric nitrogen molecules, allowing them to bond with oxygen and dissolve into rainwater as nitrates, nature’s own fertiliser, delivered directly to the soil. For billions of years, this has been one of the primary ways the Earth replenishes nitrogen in its ecosystems.Now, engineers have figured out how to bottle that process, and farmers are beginning to take notice.

What is Green Lightning?Over a decade ago, Joe Lewis, an engineer from Florida, discovered what has come to be called “Green Lightning nitrogen” as a byproduct while working on hydrogen engines. The technology makes use of nitrates created in the same way as during lightning storms, putting them into a form that can be applied directly to crops.

The Green Lightning machine replicates what happens naturally in our environment. During a lightning storm, static electricity rearranges the nitrogen molecules in the atmosphere and attaches them to raindrops. The machine creates lightning in a controlled environment under the same premise, sending air and purified water into a chamber and through an electrostatic field, where nitrogen in the air is combined with oxygen in the water to produce NO3 and NO2 molecules. The resulting product looks, feels, and weighs the same as water.Developed by U.S. company Green Lightning Solutions, the machine uses plasma arc reactors to split nitrogen molecules in the air, mimicking the chemical reaction that occurs between lightning and rain.

The economicsThe financial argument for Green Lightning is what has turned the most heads in the farming community.

Green Lightning can produce nitrogen at a rate of 4–6 cents per pound, compared to conventional synthetic nitrogen production which costs between 65 cents and a dollar per pound.Once you factor in additional costs such as the machine itself, a reverse osmosis water treatment system, and storage, the cost of nitrogen rises to around 13–22 cents per pound, still a significant saving over traditional inputs.In the United States, machines come in three sizes: a single-head system producing 17 gallons per day suited for gardens or small trials, the Thunder 365 producing 100 gallons per day (the most popular option), and the GL-Mega Filling Station producing 500 gallons per day for large farm operations.

How its appliedOne of the technology’s practical strengths is how easily it integrates into existing farming operations.

The product is essentially water with elevated levels of nitrate/nitrogen. It can be used as a fertiliser through foliar application (spraying it on crops) but can also be applied into the ground at planting time.One of the most seamless integration points is using Green Lightning water as the carrier liquid in boom sprayers, replacing the plain water that would ordinarily be used to mix chemicals. If a farmer is doing a 10-gallon-per-acre herbicide pass, filling the spray tank with Green Lightning product instead of water means putting down an equivalent of 30 pounds of nitrogen on that spray pass at no extra time or labour cost. This is precisely the approach being trialled by ART Farm here in Pomona, where Green Lightning water is being mixed with chemicals in their boom sprayers, effectively delivering nitrogen as part of every spraying operation rather than as a separate fertiliser application.Through irrigation and centre pivots, some farmers are replacing 50, 60, even 70 percent of their nitrogen needs.Research suggests that spoon-feeding the crop nitrogen throughout the growth cycle is most effective - for example, three applications at 10 gallons per acre produces better results than a single application at 30 gallons per acre.

What the US trials are showingEarly field results have been promising, though the science is still catching up with the enthusiasm.

At the PTI Farm in Illinois, corn that received Green Lightning nitrogen yielded 281 bushels per acre, compared to 267 bushels per acre with conventional 32% nitrogen at 180 pounds per acre, a gain of 14 bushels per acre.In comparing Green Lightning as a replacement for traditional nitrogen whether at a 50%, 75%, or 100% rate, crop yields have been either on par with, exceeding, or just below the synthetic nitrogen rate.Olds College in Canada is studying nitrogen uptake from fertiliser produced by a Green Lightning unit at its Smart Farm research facility. The three-year project involves 48 crop plots and a rotation of wheat, barley, and canola.In Canada alone, approximately 150 six-head units are currently operating across about 65 farms, with nine new 30-head containerised models also being deployed to increase daily production capacity.

ANuffield Scholarship, offered through the Nuffield Farming Scholarships Trust, is one of the most respected professional development programmes in global agriculture. Established in 1947 in the United Kingdom, it was created to develop forward-thinking leaders within the agricultural sector by encouraging international study, innovation and the exchange of ideas. While the programme has strong historical roots in Commonwealth countries, it has since evolved into a far broader international network, with scholars and partner programmes now spanning Europe, the Americas and beyond.

Unlike a traditional academic qualification, a Nuffield Scholarship is a self-directed research and travel opportunity. Scholars select a topic they are passionate about and spend time exploring it on a global scale. This often involves travelling for several weeks across multiple countries, meeting farmers, researchers, agribusiness leaders and policymakers, and gaining first-hand insight into how different systems operate. The experience culminates in a detailed report and a series of presentations, allowing scholars to share their findings and contribute knowledge back into their home industries.The programme is typically structured in three phases. Scholars begin by attending an international conference, where they are introduced to a global network of peers and exposed to key issues facing agriculture worldwide. This is followed by a group travel component, often referred to as the Global Focus Programme, where participants visit a range of countries to gain a broad understanding of global agricultural systems. The final phase is an individual study tour, during which each scholar undertakes in-depth research into their chosen topic.Nuffield Scholarships are aimed at individuals working within agriculture or related sectors, not limited to farmers alone. Applicants are generally mid-career professionals who demonstrate leadership potential and a strong desire to make a meaningful impact within their industry.Scholars benefit from leadership development, mentorship and access to an extensive international alumni network. This network, coordinated globally through Nuffield International Farming Scholars, remains one of the programme’s most valuable aspects, fostering collaboration and ongoing exchange of ideas long after the scholarship has concluded.The impact of a Nuffield Scholarship is often far-reaching. Many alumni go on to influence agricultural policy, lead agribusinesses, or drive innovation within their respective fields. By exposing participants to global perspectives and encouraging critical thinking, the programme helps bring new ideas back to local farming systems, ultimately strengthening the resilience and sustainability of agriculture.

The programme in ZimbabweAdding to the programme’s growing global footprint, February 2027 will see Zimbabwe host a major milestone event. The Contemporary Scholars Conference (CSC) for the new 2027 intake will take place in Victoria Falls, bringing together scholars from around the world for a week of engagement, learning and networking. The event is expected to showcase Zimbabwe’s agricultural sector on an international stage and promises to be a particularly exciting moment for the local industry.

ApplicationsAny queries can be directed to the secretary at nuffieldzimbabwe@gmail.comOnce the Nuffield Zimbabwe selection panel has formally interviewed selected applicants, the successful candidate will need to personally contribute funds (personal or through own sponsorship) sufficient to cover the cost of travel to the Contemporary Scholars Conference. Attendance at this conference is compulsory. They also participate in a Global Focus programme. This includes 4-5 weeks of worldwide international travel with six programme options. There is also required participation in a four-week self-organised study programme with individual research. Upon return to Zimbabwe, a report on the study topic is submitted and a verbal presentation is made to Nuffield Zimbabwe and sponsors.

After a break in the programme (the last scholar from Zimbabwe was selected in 2002), a committee formed in 2018 has undertaken to revive the Nuffield Zimbabwe Farming Scholars Trust. Since then, 12 scholars have been selected: Phil Weller (2019), Ranga Huruba (2020), alongside Yvonne Dzuda, Johan Odendaal, Sandi Roberts, Graeme Sharp (2022), Qa Khumalo and Robert Davy (2023), Steve Pocock (2024), Beth Goodwin (2025) and Sarah Whaley and Colette Kirk in 2026.

Crop rotation is an agronomic practice with beneficial effects that include lowering the incidence of weeds, insects, and plant diseases as well as improvements in soil physical, chemical, and biological properties. Improvements in the soil’s physical properties include better water-holding capacity and aggregate stability and improvements in the biological properties include an increase inorganic matter which then replenishes soil nitrogen (N) and carbon. This practice is among the most effective and sustainable pest and disease management practices in tobacco production. However, the common rotations traditionally used in tobacco production have relied on the use of long-season relay crops or three to four-year grass leys for example using Katambora grass. While this was practical, currently they are difficult to successfully implement as the predominantly small-scale growers do not have enough land to practice the recommended long rotations such as the 3-4 years of a grass ley. It has, therefore, become necessary to develop shorter rotations with non-host relay crops. This paper will advise growers on the ideal approach to managing soil health for different situations where full rotations cannot be done.

1. Shorter season G HR1 Grass leyThe Tobacco Research Board, Zimbabwe, developed a superior Katambora grass cultivar (G HR1) with a higher nematode suppression effect (Fig 1). Its resistance to the pest is markedly higher than that of the old purple-headed Katambora Rhodes grass and much more so than that of the Giant Rhodes grass. More importantly, G HR1 appears to suppress nematode populations in a shorter rotation period (6-12 months) than the old Katambora Rhodes grass variety which required 3-4 years.

Figure 1: Rotation using G HR 1 Katambora grass variety in tobacco lands2. Sunn hempSunn hemp(Crotalaria juncea L.)is an ideal green manure cover crop for rotations between continuous tobacco. It also has a very marked effect on weed suppression, both during growth by smothering them and as dead cover through shading and allelopathy – the effect of chemical substances released during the growth or breakdown of certain plants, which inhibits the germination or development of others.Figure 2: Sunn hemp (Crotalaria juncea L) cropSunn hemp is a poor host to many plant-parasitic nematodes and is capable of producing allelopathic (toxic) compounds, that suppress the common root-knot nematode (RKN)(Meloidogyne javanica). This makes it an efficient cover-crop for RKN management. Besides suppressing RKNs directly, sunn hemp amendments have been demonstrated to enhance free-living nematodes in the soil that are involved in nutrient cycling, thus increasing nutrients available for plant uptake. A healthier crop is more tolerant to RKN damage. However, caution must be taken as sunn hemp is a legume and can increase nitrogen level in the soil. Soil analysis for fertilizer recommendations before growing tobacco is strongly advised. Additionally, sunn hemp is vulnerable to Fusarium wilt caused byFusarium oxysporum, with no damage in the sunn hemp and lethal damage in the tobacco crop. It is, therefore, important to ensure that the seed used for rotation crops is treated, for example, withTrichoderma harzianum(T77) so that it does not harbour seed-borne pathogens, which may lead to field contamination.3. Biofumigation using Mustard and related Brassica spp.Biofumigation (BF) is the agronomic practice of using allelopathic compounds, released from decomposing Brassica tissues, to suppress soil-borne pests and pathogens. The most common allelopathic compounds produced during the breakdown of Brassica plants are isothiocyanates (ITCs). ITCs are related to the active ingredient in the commercialfumigant metham sodium and dazomet and are highly toxic to pests and pathogens. They are released following tissue damage and it is believed their evolutionary role is to provide resistance against pests and pathogens.Figure 3: Brassica plantsBiofumigation using mustard and related leafy vegetable species is a practical option as production of these vegetables is already popular for local growers. Mustard production in Zimbabwe, along with other traditional African vegetables, is on the rise due to its high nutritional value and potential as a source of income. In addition to root-knot nematode management, other benefits of including Brassicas as rotation crops include (1) altering soil ecology resulting in different rates of nutrient uptake by plants; (2) improvement in soil physical structure by increasing soil porosity if used as green manure; (3) Addition of more organic carbon to the soil which is needed to increase the activity of functional groups within the soil; (4) targets a broad spectrum of pathogens but does not persist in the soil for long periods because of the high reactivity of ITCs.

This practice may hold promise as a management tool for small-scale tobacco growers who may not have the capacity to conduct chemical fumigations in the field.

4. OtherCurrent research on suitable relay crops for tobacco at TRB includes work on the use of crops such as chia, industrial hemp, velvet beans and silverleaf desmodium. These crops will not only rehabilitate the soil and manage pests and diseases but are also important as cash crops.

Thus, used in combination with resistant varieties and recommended cultural control practices, tobacco ‘short’ rotations remain a promising management option for RKNs in tobacco in Zimbabwe.
