Tyres play a critical role in the safety, handling, and efficiency of any vehicle or machine. Proper tyre maintenance not only extends tyre life but also reduces operating costs and helps prevent accidents caused by tyre failure. From correct storage and handling to proper inflation and safe fitting procedures, understanding how to look after tyres is essential for drivers, fleet operators, and workshop personnel alike.

Tyre Use and MaintenanceGood tyre maintenance starts long before the tyre is fitted to a vehicle. Tyres should always be kept clean and stored away from heat, direct light, ozone, and hydrocarbon sources. Prolonged exposure to sunlight can accelerate rubber degradation, reducing tyre strength over time. Tyres must never come into contact with grease, petrol, volatile solvents, or other chemicals that can damage rubber compounds.

Storage methods are equally important. Tubeless tyres should not be stored horizontally, except for small-size tyres, which may be stacked or stored flat for a maximum of six months. When tyres are stored flat, they should be positioned lug against lug. For tyres fitted on rims and placed in storage, inflation pressure should be reduced to avoid unnecessary stress. Tyres must always be free of internal moisture and should never be stored directly on the ground for extended periods.

Repairs to TyresFor safety reasons, tyre repairs should only be carried out by trained specialists using the correct tools and approved methods. Incorrect or poorly executed repairs compromise tyre integrity and can pose serious risks during operation. When in doubt, damaged tyres should be removed from service and inspected by qualified professionals.Proper Use of TyresCorrect tyre use depends on understanding the relationship between speed, inflation pressure, and load capacity. Overloading a tyre places excessive stress on its structure and results in premature failure. Manufacturer technical documentation and inflation tables should always be used to determine the correct pressures for specific loads and operating speeds.

Under-inflation leads to increased heat buildup, uneven or rapid tread wear, ply separation, and eventual structural damage. Over-inflation, on the other hand, makes the tyre overly stiff, reduces its ability to absorb impacts, and increases the risk of ply tears when the tyre strikes obstacles.

Fitting and Removal: A Critical Safety IssueTyre fitting and removal procedures can be extremely dangerous if not carried out correctly. These tasks must only be performed by trained and qualified personnel using proper tools and equipment. Failure to follow recommended procedures can lead to incorrect tyre seating and, in severe cases, explosive tyre failure that may result in serious injury or death.

Before fitting, it is essential to ensure that the tyre, rim, and tube are compatible and suitable for the intended machine. Only rims recommended or permitted by the tyre manufacturer should be used. Rims must be clean and free from cracks, distortion, or welded repairs. Both the inside and outside of the tyre should be thoroughly inspected, and any tyre with irreparable damage should be scrapped.When tubes are used, the correct new tube and flap must always be fitted. For tubeless tyres mounted on tubeless rims, a new tubeless valve is required. Approved tyre lubricants should be applied to the rim and beads—never silicone or petroleum-based products. Vertical fitting is recommended, as horizontal fitting makes it difficult to confirm correct bead seating.During inflation, the valve core should be removed to allow controlled airflow and proper bead seating. Inflation must be carried out slowly, using a safety cage or restraints, while keeping a safe distance. Pressure should not exceed 36 psi if the beads are not correctly seated. If seating is incorrect, the tyre must be deflated, lubricated again, and reinflated until properly aligned. Final pressure should always be set according to the load requirements.When removing a tyre, beads must never be unseated while the tyre is inflated. Farm’s banana enterprise gave the family confidence to proceed.

“The success of the banana project, in an area not ideal for bananas, gave us the confidence that our farm has a microclimate that would support a macadamia orchard,” he said.The first macadamia plantings began in late 2019, with the orchard progressively developed in three stages and now covering 145 hectares. Four main varieties have been established across the orchard: A4, 814, 816 and Beaumont.Macadamias thrive in warm, humid conditions, making climate assessment a critical factor before planting.“We have good heat thresholds for macadamias to thrive, but the lack of humidity during October and November can cause problems,” said Rouse. “This is where investment into irrigation has been very important.”Given the farm’s climate and rainfall patterns, irrigation was considered essential from the outset. The system incorporates several principles associated with regenerative agriculture and contributes to overall orchard health.Like many farming enterprises in Zimbabwe, the project faces environmental and operational risks.“Fire is a major concern in our area, and protecting our perimeter is a challenge,” Rouse noted.The region’s hot, dry conditions during September, October and November can also create difficulties for macadamia production.“The hot dry period can cause nut drop and loss of yield,” he explained.Despite these challenges, the family remains optimistic about the future of the crop and the global market.“The market is recovering from a historic collapse,” said Rouse. “Oversupply is slowing the recovery, but the market growth is healthy and should soon counter the oversupply, hopefully creating stronger pricing in the future.”Export markets remain central to the project’s viability.“These markets are our biggest target, and they are essential for viability,” he said.

Beyond primary production, the Rouse family is also focused on increasing local value addition. A significant portion of the crop is being retained for cracking, roasting, salting, packaging and branding within Zimbabwe, with products intended for both local and export markets.Looking ahead, the Rouses believe Zimbabwe’s macadamia sector has strong potential, provided growers have access to the right support structures.“We need better marketing of Zimbabwean macadamia brands, as well as security for long-term investment and improved access to finance,” said Rouse.He also emphasised the importance of working with reputable technical partners.“I would recommend macadamias to other farmers in similar regions, provided they can ensure good establishment with irrigation, quality seedlings, and partner with reputable service providers for fertiliser and chemicals,” he said.Romwe Farm has worked closely with Hybrid Agri on integrated pest management and Kynoch on fertiliser and nutrition programmes.The farming approach adopted at Chiminya River Macadamias has also created an environment where wildlife continues to flourish. Healthy populations of sable, nyala and bushbuck move through the orchard, while abundant birdlife remains a feature of the farm.Asked what the greatest lesson from the Chiminya River Macadamias project has been so far, Rouse answered simply: “Patience.”Over the next five years, the family hopes to achieve yields of around three tonnes per hectare across the 145-hectare orchard, a milestone that would firmly establish macadamias as a successful addition to the Romwe farming enterprise.“This is a long-term investment that’s pushing us into new territory,” said Rouse. “Diversification is key to building resilience in modern farming.”

The Rouse family are quick to credit Mark Kidson for his role in the success of the developing orchard.

“Mark has been central to the growing and management of the macadamias on the ground,” they said. “The project would not be where it is today without his dedication, knowledge and day-to-day commitment to the orchard.”

This article provides a deeper analysis of the commercial 2.5-year steer production model previously described in Optimising Beef Production Systems and later referenced in the comparison article Economics of Pedigree Cattle Production: Pedigree vs Commercial Production. The purpose is to examine the practical economics of a commercial beef enterprise in greater detail, particularly the relationship between cattle value, working capital requirements, and returns.

The model presented is based on a 100 AU system (AU = Animal Units), averaging approximately 137 head carried over the production cycle, using assumptions aligned with recommended Zimbabwean beef production benchmarks, including supplementation levels, reproductive and growth performance targets.A particular focus of this analysis is the inclusion of opening working capital requirements, a factor often overlooked when evaluating beef enterprises. Grazingland has been accounted for through a rental value of $2 per head per month. While livestock, grazing, and operating capital are included in the calculations, this should not be viewed as a total Return on Investment (ROI) analysis, as certain capital assets such as tractors, vehicles, and equipment, are excluded. Fixed costs are included, though these will vary by circumstance. Consequently, the figures represent production-system returns relative toopening livestock value and opening working capital.The following summarises the returns possible from one of the production and marketing routes recognised in commercial cattle production in Zimbabwe. The assumptions are based on recommended supplementation levels and production targets aligned with the Zimbabwe Beef Production Manual (for example 80% pregnancy).The model is described more fully in the presentation:Optimising Beef Production Systems(1). The 2.5 Year model was used as a comparison in the article Economics of Pedigree Cattle Production (2).

Profit is represented as an 8.2% return on opening working capital and animal value: $53 per head on an investment of $644. This is reflected in Chart 4.Chart 4On a Gross Margin basis returns calculate to 19.5 % of working capital and livestock value, after the Fixed Costs allowed for in the assumptions, a return of 8.2% results,  this may appear modest, however, when viewed through the lens of compounding, under the ‘Rule of 72,’ reinvesting at this rate would double the initial investment in approximately 8.78 years (72/8.2).

These results are based on assumptions in a developing bio-economic optimisation model that has been back-tested in practice and has proven realistic in its multi-year form. It has shown a consistent correlation between projections and actual outcomes in an upward trend and the compounding of capital.Actual results will vary; however, this model provides a mathematically optimal solution aligned with Zimbabwean Beef Production benchmarks. Costs are largely 2025 -based, while prices reflect the current trends (2026). The structure in terms of opening animal value, opening working capital, profit analysis, and expressing costs and returns on a per head or animal unit basis and as a percentage of opening working capital and animal value (direct capital invested) can be used as a guideline for decision making and standardised comparison.

ANuffield Scholarship, offered through the Nuffield Farming Scholarships Trust, is one of the most respected professional development programmes in global agriculture. Established in 1947 in the United Kingdom, it was created to develop forward-thinking leaders within the agricultural sector by encouraging international study, innovation and the exchange of ideas. While the programme has strong historical roots in Commonwealth countries, it has since evolved into a far broader international network, with scholars and partner programmes now spanning Europe, the Americas and beyond.

Unlike a traditional academic qualification, a Nuffield Scholarship is a self-directed research and travel opportunity. Scholars select a topic they are passionate about and spend time exploring it on a global scale. This often involves travelling for several weeks across multiple countries, meeting farmers, researchers, agribusiness leaders and policymakers, and gaining first-hand insight into how different systems operate. The experience culminates in a detailed report and a series of presentations, allowing scholars to share their findings and contribute knowledge back into their home industries.The programme is typically structured in three phases. Scholars begin by attending an international conference, where they are introduced to a global network of peers and exposed to key issues facing agriculture worldwide. This is followed by a group travel component, often referred to as the Global Focus Programme, where participants visit a range of countries to gain a broad understanding of global agricultural systems. The final phase is an individual study tour, during which each scholar undertakes in-depth research into their chosen topic.Nuffield Scholarships are aimed at individuals working within agriculture or related sectors, not limited to farmers alone. Applicants are generally mid-career professionals who demonstrate leadership potential and a strong desire to make a meaningful impact within their industry.Scholars benefit from leadership development, mentorship and access to an extensive international alumni network. This network, coordinated globally through Nuffield International Farming Scholars, remains one of the programme’s most valuable aspects, fostering collaboration and ongoing exchange of ideas long after the scholarship has concluded.The impact of a Nuffield Scholarship is often far-reaching. Many alumni go on to influence agricultural policy, lead agribusinesses, or drive innovation within their respective fields. By exposing participants to global perspectives and encouraging critical thinking, the programme helps bring new ideas back to local farming systems, ultimately strengthening the resilience and sustainability of agriculture.

The programme in ZimbabweAdding to the programme’s growing global footprint, February 2027 will see Zimbabwe host a major milestone event. The Contemporary Scholars Conference (CSC) for the new 2027 intake will take place in Victoria Falls, bringing together scholars from around the world for a week of engagement, learning and networking. The event is expected to showcase Zimbabwe’s agricultural sector on an international stage and promises to be a particularly exciting moment for the local industry.

ApplicationsAny queries can be directed to the secretary at nuffieldzimbabwe@gmail.comOnce the Nuffield Zimbabwe selection panel has formally interviewed selected applicants, the successful candidate will need to personally contribute funds (personal or through own sponsorship) sufficient to cover the cost of travel to the Contemporary Scholars Conference. Attendance at this conference is compulsory. They also participate in a Global Focus programme. This includes 4-5 weeks of worldwide international travel with six programme options. There is also required participation in a four-week self-organised study programme with individual research. Upon return to Zimbabwe, a report on the study topic is submitted and a verbal presentation is made to Nuffield Zimbabwe and sponsors.

After a break in the programme (the last scholar from Zimbabwe was selected in 2002), a committee formed in 2018 has undertaken to revive the Nuffield Zimbabwe Farming Scholars Trust. Since then, 12 scholars have been selected: Phil Weller (2019), Ranga Huruba (2020), alongside Yvonne Dzuda, Johan Odendaal, Sandi Roberts, Graeme Sharp (2022), Qa Khumalo and Robert Davy (2023), Steve Pocock (2024), Beth Goodwin (2025) and Sarah Whaley and Colette Kirk in 2026.

To find out more, visit the Dudutech stand (Phil Weller) at the ADMA Show.
